title: Saying "slow down" politely
summary: A limit per client stops one noisy caller or a flood from taking everyone down.

steps.title: A bouncer, not a wall
steps.text: One buggy script or an attacker can send more requests than the whole crowd. A rate limiter counts requests per client and answers the extra ones with a quick "too many requests" (HTTP 429). Everyone else is served as usual.

steps.prompt: A flood of junk traffic is hitting the servers. Add a rate limiter in front.

between.note: The limiter goes in front of the servers, between the browser and them, so junk is stopped early. Drop it onto that line.

steps.hint: Place a Rate limiter between the browser and the servers. Try a limit of 100 requests per second per client.

steps.title: How it counts
steps.text: A token bucket gives each client tokens that refill at a steady rate; each request spends one. A short burst is fine, a long flood runs dry. If the limiter itself is down you choose: fail open (let everyone in) or fail closed (let nobody in).

rows.label: Typical API limit
rows.value: ≈ 1 to 100 requests a second per key
rows.how: free public tiers are often about 5,000 an hour (1.4 a second); paid tiers far more, approx.

steps.q: What does a rate limiter send back to an over-limit client?
choices: A 500 server error and an apology
Nothing, so the client waits forever

steps.q: If the limiter fails, "fail open" means:
choices: Restart all the servers at once
Send every request to a queue
steps.why: Open favors availability; closed favors protection.

steps.q: Why limit per client, not just in total?
choices: It is far easier to build and to run
One client cannot eat everyone's share
Totals cannot be counted across servers
It makes every request run faster
steps.why: A total cap punishes everyone for one bad caller.

takeaway: Limit each caller so one flood cannot become everyone's outage.
